summary: Menagerie Island light at the mouth of Siskiwit Bay, Lake Superior: lit in 1875, kept by resident keepers until its 1914 automation, and the Malone family's three decades on the island.

lens.where: replaced by a 12-volt solar acrylic optic (NPS)

structures.note: 61 ft (NPS, LighthouseFriends); double-walled; outer wall whitewashed
Rectangular, 28 by 45 ft, eight rooms; joined to the tower by a covered passage (NPS). Build year from the USLHS record.
Small shelter outside the tower base for two spare acetylene tanks, part of the October 1928 stand-by installation (Lighthouse Service Bulletin 1929).

access.note: Reachable only by private boat (NPS). Grounds open, tower closed (LighthouseFriends).

events.note: Congress appropriates $20,000 for a lighthouse on Isle Royale, 3 March 1873 (LighthouseFriends; not checked against the Statutes)
Octagonal red sandstone tower and keepers' dwelling completed; the NPS says the light was completed and operative in 1875
Placed in operation 20 September 1875, William Stevens head keeper
John H. Malone takes charge after swapping stations with William Stevens
Hail, snow and rain, a tempest; the station's boat, boathouse ways and dock lost (keeper's log as quoted by LighthouseFriends)
Steamer Algoma ran aground on Mott Island, near the east end of Isle Royale, on 7 November 1885 and broke in two. Not at the station; the keeper logged it.
John A. Malone, son, takes charge as head keeper
John H. Malone transfers to the Pipe Island light on the St. Marys River
Changed from a fixed to a flashing character (Lighthouse Service Bulletin 1914)
Changed to automatic acetylene in May 1914; keepers' service discontinued (Bulletin 1929; LighthouseFriends dates it 29 May 1914). Oil to acetylene in the same change.
Stand-by acetylene light installed in October 1928, with duplicate burner and spare gas supply
John H. Malone, retired keeper, dies on 8 December 1928
Battery-powered lighting system replaces the acetylene equipment
National Park Service installs a new roof on the keeper's dwelling
Solar-powered light installed atop the lighthouse (LighthouseFriends); the NPS describes a 12-volt solar acrylic optic

wrecks.outcome: Ran aground on Mott Island near the east end of Isle Royale and broke in two; 14 survivors picked up by the Athabasca. Toll reported as 100 (an early newspaper report, 13 Nov 1885), 48 (a Saginaw headline quoted by the NPS) and 46 (LighthouseFriends).
wrecks.note: Not at the station; the keeper logged it and found four life preservers on the beach abreast the station in June 1886.

corrections.why: The Park Service and LighthouseFriends both give a focal plane of 75 feet (22.9 m) above mean low water; the record's 21.9 m may use a different datum.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Park Service summary gives 1913 and its history 1939. The 1914 Bulletin (fixed to flashing, oil to acetylene), the 1929 Bulletin (services discontinued when changed to automatic acetylene in May 1914) and LighthouseFriends (29 May 1914) agree on 1914, and the roster's keeper lines end that year. The story follows them and says so.

The 1929 Bulletin obituary says Malone entered the service in 1877 and was at Isle Royale from 1878 to 1910. The roster gives 1878. LighthouseFriends has him at the Portage Lake Ship Canal light from 1877 until the 1878 swap, which reconciles the two.

The Park Service says up to 11 children; LighthouseFriends counts a dozen, one of whom died at birth. The 1925 Bulletin gives 12 for an unnamed keeper. The first two can both hold for Malone; the Bulletin does not name him.

notes_for_editor: Sources read: Park Service page for the light (cite 1); U.S. Lighthouse Society place record and roster, 18 lines (cite 2); Lighthouse Service Bulletins 1914 p. 27, 1925 p. 43 (printed p. 101), and 1929 pp. 6-7 (cites 3-6; the 1929 stand-by article and the obituary were read from the page text); LighthouseFriends (cite 7; secondary, used for facts and one short logbook quotation); the Park Service Algoma article, which reprints 1885 newspapers and the master's statement (cite 8); and the Springfield weekly Republican of 13 November 1885, p. 4, via Chronicling America (cite 9). Putnam's 1917 general history was read but is not cited: it repeats the 1925 Bulletin anecdote and says the inspector told the keeper he wanted a married man, where the Bulletin says the superintendent did. The guide keeps general histories to general context, so that difference is recorded here, not in the story. Not checked: NRHP 83000880 (the nomination is not digitised; the PDF is the 76-character placeholder); the 1873 appropriation in the Statutes (Lighthouse Board reports before 1891 are not in the local corpus); the Algoma toll beyond the 1885 Springfield report and the Park Service reprints. Disagreements left in the story: the Algoma toll (100 in the Springfield report of 13 November 1885; 48 in a Saginaw headline of 11 November as the Park Service reprints it; 46 dead in LighthouseFriends); the automation year (1913 and 1939 on the Park Service page; 1914 in the Bulletins and LighthouseFriends); and the unnamed keeper of the 1925 Bulletin, whom LighthouseFriends ties to John H. Malone. That link rests on LighthouseFriends alone, because the Bulletin names no one. The 1929 Bulletin passages are OCR, and the burner size in the stand-by light is left out because the OCR garbles it. The station's position in the record (47.9478, -88.7613, from OpenStreetMap) is 0.66 km from the USLHS place position; the record's position is kept. The keeper roster's person slugs match roster.py output. Mary Ann Stevens is recorded as first assistant, as the roster and LighthouseFriends give her. The record's characteristic (Fl W 6s) and range (7.8 nmi) are not confirmed by these sources; the Park Service gives its optic's beam as 10 miles without naming a unit, so the range is left unchanged.
